title: Is Your Lesson Feedback Actually a Google Review
author: Dr Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele argues that unannounced, one-way lesson-observation feedback works like a customer's Google review: the observer prepared notes while the exhausted teacher is expected to recall and defend micro-decisions on the spot. He frames this as an asymmetrical trial that erodes self-efficacy and turns professional development into an audit. His remedy is for teachers to claim a right to reply by requesting reflection time, asking probing questions about policy and frameworks, and checking the school's teaching model. He backs the case with Coe et al. on observation unreliability, Kluger and DeNisi on feedback that harms performance, Sweller on cognitive load, and Kraft, Blazar and Hogan on coaching. The move is to recast feedback as a two-way dialogue and give teachers practical scripts for it.
points: One-way observation feedback imposes a cognitive load imbalance, since the observer prepared notes while the teacher must recall hours-old micro-decisions.
The unannounced debrief becomes a trial in which the teacher is forced to act as their own lawyer and may concede things they did not think or do.
Teachers can claim a right to reply by asking for time to reflect and by questioning which policy or framework the feedback is measured against.
Research cited shows snapshot observations are unreliable and that over a third of feedback interventions decrease performance.
Ongoing collaborative instructional coaching, rather than one-off reviews, is what shifts teaching quality and student outcomes.
quotes: You are experiencing a one-way feedback review, and it operates remarkably like a Google review left on a restaurant’s profile by a customer who recently dined in.

The observer spent 20 minutes sitting comfortably at the back of your room, taking detailed notes on a snapshot of a single lesson. You, meanwhile, were actively managing a live room of thirty teenagers while balancing complex working memory demands.
Because you are caught off-guard, your natural defensive instincts kick in. You become your own lawyer, frantically trying to construct a defence for a 30-second interaction from earlier in the day.
When feedback is a one-way street, it ceases to be formative professional development. It becomes a audit.
Never feel forced to accept or debate feedback the moment it is handed to you.
Feedback often reflects the personal preference of the individual observer rather than the school’s actual teaching and learning framework.
Kluger and DeNisi’s landmark meta-analysis on the effects of feedback interventions showed that over one-third (38%) of feedback interventions actually decrease performance.
Professional dialogue is a two-way street, and true growth only happens when both sides are listening.
